analysis.one_liner: Bans lenders from paying mortgage brokers kickbacks for steering borrowers into higher-rate loans.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban mortgage brokers' kickbacks for steering borrowers into pricier loans never got a committee hearing or a vote in the 111th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When you get a mortgage through a broker, the lender often pays that broker a bonus — a "yield spread premium" — for landing you in a loan with a higher interest rate than the one you qualified for. That gives the person arranging your loan a financial reason to pick a worse deal for you. This bill would have made that payment illegal: no compensation to a mortgage originator could depend on the loan's terms, only on its amount. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and homeowners refinancing a mortgage. The ban would remove the hidden incentive for the broker arranging their loan to push them into a higher interest rate than they qualified for, since the broker's payday would no longer grow with the loan's cost. Borrowers who qualify for good rates would keep them, because the lender would have no way to pay the broker extra for a pricier loan.

how_it_helps.text: It barred any person from providing, and any mortgage originator from receiving, compensation based on or varying with the terms of a home mortgage loan (other than the loan amount) — eliminating the incentive to place borrowers in more expensive loans.

It covered every kind of originator — mortgage brokers, bank lenders, and anyone negotiating loan terms or sales of existing loans — on any loan secured by a home, including condos, co-ops, and manufactured homes.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and lenders. Brokers would lose yield spread premiums — lender payments for delivering loans at above-market rates — which were a significant part of broker income. Lenders would lose a tool for inducing brokers to originate higher-rate loans, and the industry would face a new prohibition on how it structures compensation.

drawbacks.text: The bill was a blanket ban: it prohibited all originator compensation tied to loan terms, with no alternative structure for how brokers would be paid, which the mortgage industry argued could reduce broker flexibility and push compensation into other forms.

A borrower who could not pay closing costs upfront sometimes used a yield spread premium to cover them in exchange for a higher rate; an outright ban removed that option without creating a substitute.
As a one-sponsor bill with no cosponsors and no committee action, it added nothing to the legislative record — no hearings, no markups — that would have tested whether the ban worked as intended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well-targeted: paying brokers more for pricier loans creates a built-in conflict of interest, and the bill would have removed it directly. The main cost is that a blanket ban on all term-based compensation, without an accompanying structure for how brokers should be paid, could make broker compensation less flexible and might have pushed some costs into upfront fees; honest supporters would acknowledge it was a blunt instrument. On balance, the protection it offered to homebuyers against hidden steering costs outweighed the adjustment burden on the mortgage industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Merkley introduced the bill on April 28, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended January 3, 2011.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point.
The bill was one page: a flat ban on compensation that varies with a home mortgage loan's terms, a practice known as yield spread premiums.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage brokers and lenders kept the yield-spread-premium channel unregulated by Congress during this period; the practice was later addressed by federal regulators under separate rulemaking, not by this bill.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was his first Congress in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the two-plus years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Chris Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, never brought the bill before the committee; the record shows no action after the April 28, 2009 referral.

against.name: Mortgage broker trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed bans on yield spread premiums during this period, arguing brokers needed the flexibility and that the payments let borrowers finance closing costs; no lobbying appears in this bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded; its sole sponsor was a Democrat and it attracted no cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: Yield spread premiums were a major income stream: lenders paid brokers extra for delivering loans at above-market rates. The bill eliminates that payment, and with it the financial incentive to steer borrowers into costlier loans. Broker trade groups fought similar bans in this period because their compensation model depended on it.

Lenders used yield spread premiums as a cheap tool to induce brokers to originate higher-rate loans; the bill removes that tool and bars them from paying it. Lenders bear little direct cost beyond losing the steering channel, but their interest in blocking the bill ran against borrowers' wallets.
Borrowers would no longer face an undisclosed conflict where the person arranging their mortgage earns more the worse the loan is for them. Not an industry, but the group the bill was written for.
